content: The treatment regimens referred to as BPALM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin), BPALC (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and clofazimine), and BPAL (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) were evaluated in clinical trials such as the ZeNix trial and the Nix-TB study. These trials provided evidence on the use of BPAL regimens with varying linezolid dosing schedules. Additionally, programmatic data from South Africa’s National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) supported the use of a new 9-month shorter treatment regimen. Evidence from other treatment regimens, used as external comparators, was also analyzed to estimate the effectiveness of these intervention regimens. The evidence included data on the WHO-recommended shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen, implemented programmatically in South Africa, and the longer WHO-recommended regimens, with data collected from country programs in Belarus, Georgia, India, Moldova, Mozambique, Papua New Guinea, the Russian Federation, and Somalia. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) provided fieldwork data from multiple countries, as well as cohort data from the EndTB project in collaboration with Partners in Health. WHO also received data from the NExT trial, a Phase 2–3 open-label randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in South Africa, which evaluated the effectiveness of a 6–9-month all-oral regimen for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) compared to the local standard of care (SoC) regimen at the time. The principal investigator and colleagues at the University of Cape Town and the South African Medical Research Council were acknowledged for sharing data. However, during the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting, it was decided that data from the NExT trial could not be used to complement discussions on the population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) framework due to the trial’s early termination and variability in the intervention regimen components. Despite this, the trial results highlighted the inferiority and significantly worse safety profile of drug-resistant TB regimens based on injectable medicines and fluoroquinolones (excluding new and repurposed drugs). Importantly, the trial demonstrated that better outcomes could be achieved with a 6-month all-oral regimen compared to traditional 9-month or longer injectable-based regimens, supporting the concept of a 6-month all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, updated in 2022, recommend a 6-month treatment regimen composed of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid (600 mg), and moxifloxacin (BPALM) over the 9-month or longer (18-month) regimens for patients with MDR/RR-TB. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty of evidence. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) for fluoroquinolones is strongly encouraged in MDR/RR-TB patients, and while it should not delay the initiation of BPALM, the results should guide whether moxifloxacin can be retained or excluded from the regimen. The rationale for this recommendation is supported by data from the TB-PRACTECAL trial (a Phase 3 RCT), which showed significantly improved treatment success rates with the 6-month BPALM regimen (89%) compared to current SoC regimens (52%), along with lower rates of treatment failure, death, and loss to follow-up. Data from the TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials also suggested fewer adverse events with a linezolid dose of 600 mg while maintaining high efficacy. The implementation of this regimen is considered feasible, acceptable, and likely to improve cost-effectiveness and equity. The TB-PRACTECAL trial, conducted in South Africa, Belarus, and Uzbekistan, included patients with microbiologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) and followed them for 72 weeks. The trial compared the BPALM regimen to locally approved SoC regimens, including 9–12-month injectable-containing regimens, 18–24-month WHO-recommended regimens (pre-2019), and 9–12-month or 18–20-month all-oral regimens. The trial was terminated early after an independent data safety and monitoring board concluded that the BPALM regimen was superior to the SoC, as additional data were unlikely to change the trial’s results. The ZeNix trial, a Phase 3 partially blinded RCT, assessed the safety and efficacy of varying doses and durations of linezolid in combination with bedaquiline and pretomanid for patients with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB and additional resistance to fluoroquinolones or those who were treatment-intolerant or nonresponsive to previous MDR/RR-TB treatment. WHO’s updated guidelines emphasize the importance of using evidence-based shorter regimens, such as BPALM, to improve treatment outcomes for MDR/RR-TB patients. These recommendations are targeted at policymakers, national TB program managers, healthcare professionals, and technical agencies involved in TB treatment and service delivery.
